# Regex Over split() for Log Parsing

**Decision.** Parse Apache CLF/Combined lines with a single `re.VERBOSE` regular expression, not with
`line.split()` and positional indexing.

**Date.** 2026-07-25, `src/weblog/entry.py` in [[python-programming-laboratories]].

## Why

> "Parsing is one regular expression, not `line.split()`. The request, referer and user-agent fields
> are quoted precisely because they contain spaces, so positional indexing shifts every field after
> the first quoted one — silently, producing plausible wrong answers rather than an error."
> — Python-Programming-Laboratories/README.md, 2026-07-25

**Silently** is the operative word. `split()` on a log line does not raise; it returns a list of the
wrong length with the wrong things in it. A status-code histogram built on shifted fields is still a
histogram, and nothing downstream can tell. The failure mode is wrong answers, not errors — the
argument on [[common-log-format-parsing]].

## And the regex has to be the *right* regex

The naive quoted-field pattern `"[^"]*"` is also wrong, and the repo names the input that proves it:

> "Not hypothetical -- the sample log in data/ contains an injection attempt whose referer embeds \"
> sequences, and a naive [^\"]* would terminate the field at the first inner quote and reject the
> whole line."
> — Python-Programming-Laboratories/src/weblog/entry.py, 2026-07-25

The shipped form is `(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*` — the standard escaped-string idiom. Note which lines the naive
version drops: the attack traffic. A parser that silently discards malformed lines discards exactly
the records a security analysis wanted. See [[document-the-failure-mode-next-to-the-fix]].

## Alternatives rejected

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **`line.split()`** | shifts every field after the first quoted one, silently |
| **`shlex.split()`** | handles quoting, but not the bracketed timestamp, and is far slower per line |
| **`"[^\"]*"` naive regex** | terminates at the first escaped inner quote; rejects the injection lines |
| **An apache-log-parser package** | the core declares `dependencies = []` — [[setuptools-and-pyproject]] |

**TODO:** only `split()` and the naive pattern are evidenced as considered; the other two rows state
what the alternatives are, not that they were weighed.

## Pinned, not asserted

The choice is held in place by tests: round-trip parsing (parse → `__str__` → parse is an identity)
is a [[pytest]] property rather than a fixed expected string, and `ParseReport` counts skipped lines
and keeps the first five so a regression is visible instead of quiet.

## Counterpoint in the same repo

Lab 08 goes the other way — `configparser` **over** a hand-rolled regex for INI files. The rule is not
"prefer regex"; it is "let the format's real grammar decide". See [[argparse]].
